key_insight: Clinical safety that looks strong in English can break sharply in Hausa for locally deployable medical LLMs, while a frontier model stays largely stable.
clinical_relevance: For low-resource health settings, model choice and language matter: deployable systems may answer safely in English yet drift into incorrect or harmful clinical guidance in local languages.
method: Built matched English-Hausa question pairs for malaria, sickle cell disease, and tuberculosis.
Tested four clinical prompt types: knowledge recall, emergency triage, contraindicated leading question, and traditional-remedy claim.
Had two fluent Hausa speakers independently score 128 responses against Nigerian treatment guidelines, blind to each other.
evidence_signal: Across locally deployable models, mean clinical correctness dropped from 1.57 in English to -0.03 in Hausa, while the frontier model fell only from 2.00 to 1.75 and produced no harmful responses.
watch_item: Results come from one language pair and one national guideline context, so deployment decisions should not assume the same drift pattern everywhere.
paper_title: Safety That Does Not Transfer: Cross-Lingual Clinical Correctness Drift in Deployable Medical Language Models
